subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

periods.activity_title: Meet the Fort: Reading the Dialogue Aloud

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Read (pp. 125–128): read the Aarav–Ananya–Chachi dialogue aloud.

time_bands.activity: Teacher leads a picture walk and brief warm-up: students observe any newspaper picture of a fort, share one word that comes to mind, then turn to Textbook pp. 125–128 to see the chapter's illustration and title.
Let us Read (pp. 125–128) — teacher reads the dialogue aloud with expression, assigning Aarav, Ananya, and Chachi roles; students follow in their books and echo key lines after each speaker's turn.
Students re-read the dialogue in triads, each taking one character's lines; teacher circulates and supports phrasing and pronunciation of words like 'Maheshwar', 'Narmada', and 'Ahilya Bai'.
Whole class closing: teacher invites two or three students to share one detail about Maheshwar Fort that surprised them, drawing purely from the dialogue just read.

periods.teacher_notes: Maheshwar Fort sits on a hill above the Narmada River and is built from special red stones from Gujarat and Rajasthan — students often struggle with these place names, so model them clearly before the triad reading. Encourage students to use the illustration on the textbook page to visualise the overhanging balconies as they read.
materials: Newspaper or printed picture of a fort (optional warm-up prop)

periods.activity_title: Thinking About the Fort: Comprehension Discussion

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think A (p. 128): answer four questions about Ahilya Bai, the fort's location, materials, and statue.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models a re-reading of the passage sections (pp. 125–128) where Chachi describes the fort's location and Queen Ahilya Bai, thinking aloud to show students how to locate answers in dialogue.

Let us Think A (p. 128) — teacher poses questions 1 and 2 aloud (Who was Ahilya Bai? Where is the fort and what makes its location special?); students discuss with a partner, then share answers; teacher affirms and extends.

Let us Think A (p. 128) — teacher poses questions 3 and 4 (materials used in building the fort; what the statue represents); students locate evidence in the dialogue, then give oral answers before writing one sentence each in their notebooks.
Class reviews written sentences together; teacher draws a quick labelled sketch on the board — fort on hill, river below, statue in front — connecting the four comprehension answers visually.

periods.teacher_notes: Students may conflate Ahilya Bai's qualities (warrior, kind ruler, builder) — prompt them to distinguish what she did for her people (temples, schools, wells) from who she was. The red stones for the fort came from Gujarat and Rajasthan, not from Madhya Pradesh itself; this detail catches many students off guard.

periods.activity_title: Listening to Maheshwari Sarees and Discussing Historical Places

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Listen (p. 131): listen to the Maheshwari sarees passage and arrange four sentences in order.

homework.task_brief: Let us Think B (p. 129): choose one question — what makes historical places interesting, or which part of the fort excites you most — and write two sentences to share next time.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the topic of Maheshwari sarees with a brief oral prompt: 'Chachi told Aarav and Ananya that Maheshwar is famous for two things — the fort and something else. What was it?' Students recall from the dialogue.

Let us Listen (p. 131) — teacher reads the Maheshwari sarees passage aloud three times at a measured pace (students keep books closed); after the third reading, teacher writes the four jumbled sentences on the board and students arrange them in order on a slip of paper.
Students compare their arrangements with a partner; teacher reads the passage a fourth time while students check their order, then the class agrees on the correct sequence together.

Teacher opens a brief whole-class discussion using Let us Think B question 1 (p. 129): 'What do you think makes historical places like Maheshwar Fort interesting?' Three or four students share; teacher listens and acknowledges each response without evaluating.

periods.teacher_notes: The passage sequence moves from pure silk → cotton introduced → reversible borders and pallus → national and international markets; students commonly reverse the first two steps, so the fourth reading gives them a chance to self-correct. The Let us Think B discussion item is treated as an open oral exchange here, not a graded response.
materials: Textbook p. 131 (teacher's copy for reading aloud)

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak A (p. 132): research and present a local historical place to the class.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models a brief spoken presentation about Maheshwar Fort itself — name of place, historical person, special feature, and how it connects to people — demonstrating the six-point structure students will use for their own place.

Let us Speak A (p. 132) — students spend time thinking and making a quick note-card about a historical place they know from home or locality: name, associated person, two special features, and why it matters to local people; teacher circulates and assists.

Students present one at a time (one minute each); classmates listen and, after each presentation, nominate the most interesting special feature they heard; teacher gives brief affirming feedback on clarity of delivery.

Teacher closes by noting that every town carries its own history the way Maheshwar carries the story of Ahilya Bai and the fort — a brief reflective wrap connecting student presentations to the chapter's theme.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who cannot recall a local historical place may speak about any heritage site, temple, or old building they have visited or seen in pictures; the point is practising structured oral presentation, not obscure historical knowledge. Keep presentations to one minute so every student gets a turn.
materials: Index cards or note slips for student planning

periods.activity_title: Odd One Out, Silent G, and Word Meanings

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn A (p. 129): circle the odd one out in four word groups; find two sets of your own.
Let us Learn B (p. 130): identify and underline words with a silent 'g' from the given list.

homework.task_brief: Let us Learn C (p. 130): match the seven words (Kindness, Bravery, Wisdom, etc.) to their meanings independently.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'smiling', 'grinning', and 'laughing' on the board and asks students what they share; establishes the idea of synonym clusters and the 'odd one out' when one word breaks the pattern.

Let us Learn A (p. 129) — teacher reads each set aloud; students circle the odd one out individually, then pairs compare and justify their choice; teacher confirms answers and asks two or three pairs to create their own synonym sets.

Let us Learn B (p. 130) — teacher writes 'design' on the board, pronounces it, and asks students whether they hear the 'g'; explains the silent letter rule, then students work individually to underline silent-g words from the nine given and read each aloud softly.
Whole-class check of silent-g words; teacher lists correct answers on the board; students self-correct and read the underlined words once more as a group to build oral familiarity with the pattern.

periods.teacher_notes: Common confusion in the odd-one-out task: 'noisy' versus 'quiet/silent/calm' — students may not see that noisy breaks the 'quiet' synonym cluster. For silent-g, 'sing' and 'king' are the typical wrong answers since the 'ng' ending looks similar to 'gn' but the 'g' there is not silent in the same way; address this contrast explicitly.

periods.activity_title: Articles in Context: A, An, The

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn C (p. 130): match seven words about Queen Ahilya Bai's qualities to their meanings.
Let us Speak B (p. 132): fill in articles (a, an, the) in the monkey-and-bag passage.

time_bands.activity: Let us Learn C (p. 130) — teacher reviews the homework match task together; students who did it check their answers against the class response, and those who did not do it complete it now while teacher reads each word (Kindness, Bravery, Wisdom, Majestic, Unique, Fierce, Dedicated) and its meaning aloud.

Teacher connects the matched words back to the dialogue: 'Chachi used words like "majestic" and "fierce" to describe Ahilya Bai — why these words and not others?' Brief oral exchange before moving to articles.

Let us Speak B (p. 132) — teacher explains article rules (a before consonant sounds, an before vowel sounds, the for specific/known nouns) using examples from the Maheshwar dialogue; students fill in the passage individually, then check in pairs.
Teacher reads the completed passage aloud; students identify two blanks they found hardest and the class discusses why those positions are tricky — consolidating the rule in context.

periods.teacher_notes: Students consistently confuse 'a' and 'an' before words starting with a vowel letter but a consonant sound (e.g. 'a university') — at Grade IV level, focus only on the straightforward vowel-letter rule. The match task (Let us Learn C) may have been done as homework; if most students have completed it, spend only a quick five minutes confirming before moving to articles.

periods.activity_title: Writing About Maheshwar Fort: Guided and Independent

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write A (p. 133): write a short description of visiting Maheshwar Fort — what you see and feel.
Let us Write B (p. 133): write a short factual paragraph on Maheshwar Fort.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models planning for Let us Write A (p. 133) on the board: a simple three-box planner — 'What I see (balconies, stones, river view)', 'What I hear/smell/touch (imagination)', 'How I feel' — students copy the planner and fill their own boxes orally with a partner.

Let us Write A (p. 133) — students write three to four sentences describing their imagined visit to Maheshwar Fort using their planner boxes; teacher circulates, prompts sensory detail, and gives brief oral feedback on phrasing.

Teacher models Let us Write B (p. 133) by writing one factual topic sentence on the board ('Maheshwar Fort is a grand fort in Madhya Pradesh built by Queen Ahilya Bai'); students draft two to three supporting factual sentences using details from the dialogue — location, building materials, Ahilya Bai's achievements.

Students share their factual paragraph with a partner for peer response — partner underlines one fact they found most interesting; two volunteers read their paragraphs to the class; teacher gives whole-class formative feedback on clarity and detail.

periods.teacher_notes: Both writing tasks are completed and self-contained within this sitting — drafting and peer response happen together so no piece needs to travel to another sitting. Students may borrow vocabulary from the dialogue (majestic, overhanging balconies, Narmada River) — encourage this as purposeful use of text language rather than copying.
materials: Board and chalk/marker for model planning

periods.activity_title: Fort Jigsaw Puzzle: Make and Play

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do (p. 134): draw a fort on cardboard, draw a puzzle grid on the back, cut into pieces, and rearrange with friends.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays the puzzle diagram from Textbook p. 134 and explains the four steps: draw a puzzle template grid on one side of the cardboard, draw a fort on the other side, cut the pieces apart, and rearrange them to reconstruct the fort.

Let us Do (p. 134), Steps I–II — students draw a simple puzzle grid on one side of their cardboard (teacher demonstrates a 3×3 or 4×3 grid) and then draw a fort silhouette on the reverse side; teacher assists students who need support with the grid proportions.

Let us Do (p. 134), Steps III–IV — students cut along the grid lines with child-safe scissors and shuffle their pieces; pairs or small groups exchange puzzles and race to reassemble each other's fort.

Teacher leads a brief sharing circle: students hold up their completed puzzle and say one thing about Maheshwar Fort they want to remember — connecting the craft activity back to the chapter's cultural content about the fort and Queen Ahilya Bai.

periods.teacher_notes: Pre-cut cardboard strips or a printed grid template help students who struggle with ruler work and keep the cutting phase from running long. The sharing circle at the close is an opportunity to revisit words like 'majestic', 'balconies', and 'Narmada' in a relaxed spoken context.
materials: Thick chart paper or cardboard (one sheet per student)

items.item_stem: In the conversation between Aarav, Ananya, and Chachi, Chachi describes where Maheshwar Fort is located. Which of the following best describes its location?

options.label: A
options.text: On a hill overlooking the Narmada River in Madhya Pradesh.

options.label: B
options.text: On the banks of the Ganga River in Rajasthan.

options.label: C
options.text: On a hilltop near the city of Ahmedabad in Gujarat.

options.label: D
options.text: In a valley beside the Yamuna River in Uttar Pradesh.

what_each_option_reveals.B: This student may have confused the building materials' source (Rajasthan) with the fort's own location.
what_each_option_reveals.C: This student may have confused Gujarat — where building stones came from — with where the fort stands.
what_each_option_reveals.D: This student may be drawing on a general association between forts and the Yamuna without reading carefully.

items.item_stem: Chachi tells Aarav and Ananya that Queen Ahilya Bai was not only a warrior but also a kind and wise ruler. Name two things she built for her people, as mentioned in the conversation.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Queen Ahilya Bai built temples, schools, and wells for her people. Any two of these three are correct.

items.source_lo: Student listens to a narrated passage and responds by sequencing information using a listen-and-order task as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Maheshwari sarees passage: silk origins, cotton introduction, reversible borders, national and international markets.
items.item_stem: Listen as your teacher reads the passage about Maheshwari sarees aloud. Then decide whether each statement is true or false.

options.text: Maheshwari sarees were first made using pure silk.
Maheshwari sarees are only available inside India.
The sarees are known for their reversible borders and pallus.
Cotton yarn was used before silk in making Maheshwari sarees.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — True: the passage states weavers originally used pure silk. 2 — False: the passage says they are available in national and international markets. 3 — True: the passage mentions unique reversible borders and pallus. 4 — False: silk came first; cotton was introduced later.

expected_elements: Mentions silk used first, cotton added later.
Names reversible borders as a special feature.
States they are sold nationally and internationally.

items.item_stem: Chachi described Maheshwar Fort using details about its name, builder, special features, and what it means to local people. Choose a historical place, building, or monument you know and tell the class three things about it: its name and location, one special feature, and why it is important to the people there.

options.text: A student's presentation must include the name and location of the place.
A student's presentation is only valid if the place is in Madhya Pradesh.
Describing what makes a monument special is part of a good oral presentation.
How a monument connects to its people is not important to mention.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — True: naming and locating the place is the first essential point. 2 — False: any historical place from any town or locality is valid. 3 — True: special features are a core part of the presentation structure. 4 — False: emotional and community connection is one of the key presentation points.

items.item_stem: Choose the correct article to fill each blank.
items.visual_stimulus:
Sentence | Correct article
_____ elephant walked slowly through the forest. | ?
She found _____ old coin near the gate. | ?
Ahilya Bai was _____ wise and kind queen. | ?
_____ Narmada River flows below Maheshwar Fort. | ?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. An (An elephant — vowel sound). 2. an (an old — vowel sound). 3. a (a wise — consonant sound). 4. The (The Narmada River — specific, known noun).
